description: Ghost Code is a team of six students passionate about space, coding, and innovation. We aim to develop creative solutions for astronaut health monitoring through teamwork, technology, and problem-solving.
summary: Crew Health Monitor is a web application designed to support astronaut health and cabin environment monitoring during long-duration space missions. It tracks vital signs, sleep, mood, and environmental conditions, classifies readings as Normal, Warning, or Critical, and prioritizes crew members based on medical urgency. It also provides pre-approved medical guidance during communication interruptions, continuously monitors health conditions, and securely stores records for synchronization with the ground team once communication is restored.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Crew Health Monitor is a web app that checks an astronaut’s daily health readings (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, oxygen, sleep, exercise and mood) and live cabin readings (CO2, oxygen, pressure, temperature, humidity and radiation). It compares each reading with a safe range and rates it normal, warning or critical, then gives an overall level, from all clear to contact the flight surgeon. Every alert comes with a plan: likely causes, steps to do now, when to check again and when to get help. When Earth can be reached, alerts and reports go to the flight surgeon. When it cannot, the app shows the stored steps at once, keeps watching the readings and saves every record on the device. When the link returns, it sends the records to the ground team.

Benefits:
Crew Health Monitor helps astronauts access predefined emergency guidance immediately, even when communication with Earth is delayed. At the same time, it enables the ground team to access and review astronauts' health records, monitor their conditions, and prioritize those who need attention first.

Intended impact:
To make long missions to the Moon and Mars safer, where signals can take up to 20 minutes and a doctor cannot always be reached.

Tools, languages, hardware and software:

We built the app with AI tools and did not write the code by hand. Claude (Anthropic) generated the code and helped with writing. v0 (Vercel) was used for the interface design. Gamma was used to make our presentation slides. ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used to help collect information from NASA’s websites, and our team checked it against the NASA sources. The app is a web page, so it is made of HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and it was published with Netlify. No special hardware was used. The readings are simulated. The team chose the idea, gave the design direction and reviewed all content. 

How it is creative:
The app has a connected mode and an offline mode, with a switch that can be used live. It has a clickable X-ray body that shows each organ’s readings, a heartbeat line and a space-themed design. It also has a full plan for each of 22 problems, with a space-specific tip for each.

Factors our team considered:
Safety: the software uses fixed, pre-written steps and never decides treatment on its own. Honesty about data: the readings are simulated, and the cabin ranges follow NASA references. Reliability: the app works without internet. Ease of use: a simple layout that a tired astronaut can read quickly. The medical steps are a prototype and need review by medical experts.
